item.title: REP. BRIAN MAST: I want unsafe truckers off our highways — and America's veterans in their seats
item.description: Freedom Haulers fast-tracks veterans into trucking while removing foreign drivers who fail English and skills tests on U.S. roads.
item.content:encoded:
One year ago this week, three Floridians senselessly lost their lives on Florida’s Turnpike near Fort Pierce due to the complete and utter recklessness of a If you are a foreign national driving a commercial truck in America, you should have to meet the same basic safety requirements as everyone else." truck driver with an illegal CDL license.

Three people died for doing nothing more than simply driving down the highway when a tractor-trailer driver made an illegal U-turn through an access point, cutting across traffic and leaving an approaching minivan with nowhere to go.

Their families will carry that loss for the rest of their lives.

ILLEGAL ALIEN FAILED CDL TEST 10 TIMES IN 2 MONTHS BEFORE FATAL FLORIDA CRASH THAT KILLED 3

We cannot bring those Americans back. But we can decide who drives on our highways and whether their senseless deaths are going to be another tragedy we forget—or a warning that finally forces us to fix a broken system.

I choose the latter.

America should not lower our standards to accommodate foreign nationals who cannot meet basic commercial-driving requirements. Full stop. Shortsighted state policies and lax federal oversight, like California issuing Non-Domiciled CDLs without rigorous verification of legal work status or language skills, are endangering each and every American citizen.

And this doesn’t have to be the case. We have the best trained drivers in the world. American veterans already possess the discipline, training, and experience needed on the road, and I can’t think of better training for our commercial trucking industry.

SEC SEAN DUFFY: FREEDOM HAULERS PUTS VETERANS IN THE DRIVERS' SEATS OF NEW CAREERS

That is what President Trump’s Freedom Haulers initiative is about, and that’s why I’m proud to introduce the bill to make it law.

Freedom Haulers recognizes something the rest of the country should have recognized long ago: military experience counts. Veterans have the discipline, precision, accountability and experience that trucking demands. Qualified veterans with military heavy-vehicle experience can use existing federal waivers to avoid redundant road testing and get into the industry faster.

Now Congress needs to make that policy permanent.

That is why I am introducing new Freedom Haulers legislation to codify the program.

TRUMP PROMOTES FREEDOM HAULERS INITIATIVE TO FAST-TRACK MILITARY VETERANS INTO TRUCKING JOBS

It is about getting Americans who served this country into the trucking industry while getting dangerous, unqualified foreign drivers off our roads. The Trump administration has made clear that Freedom Haulers is part of a broader effort to crack down on dangerous foreign drivers, restore integrity to the trucking industry, and give our veterans good-paying jobs here at home.

That’s why, with my bill and President Trump’s initiative, we will be creating a program that fast tracks American veterans into the trucking industry, allowing veterans with qualifying military driving experience to skip the CDL knowledge test, in addition to existing mechanisms that can let them bypass the road/skills test, and use veterans’ benefits to pay for CDL training.

Federal law already requires commercial drivers to speak English and read road signs, but lax enforcement has allowed drivers who scored as low as 2 out of 12 on proficiency tests onto our highways.

VIRGINIA BUS CRASH THAT KILLED FIVE INVOLVED DRIVER WHO DOESN'T SPEAK ENGLISH, SEAN DUFFY SAYS

Foreign nationals driving on our roads, who failed English proficiency tests, who can’t understand our road signs, and who don’t know the driving laws are a real problem in our country, and we don’t need to lose another American because of it.

It ends now.

We need to get unqualified and unauthorized foreign drivers off the road—and put American veterans behind the wheel.

If you are driving a commercial truck on American highways—regardless of where you were born—you must meet strict, non-negotiable safety requirements.

If you are a foreign national driving a commercial truck in America, you should have to meet the same basic safety requirements as everyone else.

TRUMP ADMIN TRUCKING CRACKDOWN LANDS 51 IMMIGRATION DETENTIONS, 36 ENGLISH LANGUAGE PROFICIENCY VIOLATIONS

If you cannot demonstrate English proficiency, you should not be behind the wheel of an 80,000-pound vehicle. If you cannot pass the required skills test, you should not have a commercial driver's license. If you are improperly licensed, improperly authorized or otherwise fail the requirements of federal law, you should be taken off the road.

This isn't complicated.

It isn't anti-immigrant.

It isn't unfair.

It's common sense.

DEADLY ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT TRUCK CRASH EXPOSED FAILURES ON THE ROAD AND AT THE BORDER: KEY SENATOR

American families should not have to share the highway with someone who cannot communicate with law enforcement or demonstrate that they can safely operate a commercial vehicle.

The tragedy in Fort Pierce, that happened just a few miles from my home, showed why that matters.

According to the facts, the driver, who entered our country illegally, had scored just 2 out of 12 on an English proficiency test but was still given a CDL license by California. He was also operating a commercial tractor-trailer despite failing to obtain a work authorization.

TRUMP TAPS VETERANS TO FIX ILLEGAL ALIEN TRUCKING PROBLEM PLAGUING US ROADWAYS

That should never happen again.

We should not be bending the rules for people who fail them.

We should be enforcing the rules—and then giving Americans who have already proven themselves an opportunity to do the job.

That is where our veterans come in.

For years, we asked American service members to operate massive military vehicles carrying troops, fuel and equipment in some of the most dangerous environments on Earth. We trusted them with millions of dollars of equipment. We trusted them with the lives of their fellow Americans.

ARMY VET, TRUCKING EXECUTIVE RAVES OVER TRUMP PLAN TO BOLSTER BLUE COLLAR INDUSTRY BY FAST-TRACKING VETERANS

While programs exist to waive the driving test for some veterans, bureaucratic hurdles and inconsistent state rules still make them jump through unnecessary hoops, including redundant written exams. We should cut that red tape completely.

We should be removing barriers for American veterans—not lowering standards for foreign drivers.

We should be recruiting the Americans who have already demonstrated that they can do the job—not importing people who cannot meet the minimum requirements to do it safely.

And we should be making one thing absolutely clear: A commercial driver's license is not a participation trophy.

It is permission to operate a machine weighing tens of thousands of pounds alongside American families.

That privilege comes with an enormous responsibility.

If you fail the English test, you're off the road.

If you fail the skills test, you're off the road.

If your license was improperly issued, you're off the road.

If you are not legally authorized to hold the credential that allows you to operate a commercial vehicle, you're off the road.

There should be no loopholes. No excuses. No second set of standards.

And when those drivers are removed, we should fill those seats with Americans who earned the right to be there.

Our veterans have already answered the call.

They've driven military trucks.

They've followed orders.

They've operated under pressure.

Now we should give them another mission: Keep America moving.

The anniversary of the Fort Pierce crash is a reminder of what happens when we continue to let dangerous people go on our roads.

We owe those three victims more than thoughts and prayers.

We owe their families action.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

That means enforcing the rules against foreign nationals who cannot meet our standards. It means making sure every commercial driver can communicate in English and demonstrate the skills necessary to safely operate a big rig. And it means opening the door for American veterans who have already demonstrated those abilities.

We don't need to lower the bar.

We need to enforce it.

We don't need to look overseas for qualified drivers while qualified Americans are standing at the door.

We need to put our veterans behind the wheel.

Get unqualified foreign drivers off America's roads.

Put American veterans behind the wheel.

And make our highways safe again.

item.title: Four ways to harden America's power grid before our global enemies strike
item.description: The U.S. must remove Chinese inverters from its power grid and harden critical infrastructure as Iran, China, and Russia target domestic energy supplies.
item.content:encoded:
Since World War II, the U.S. military has benefitted from uncontested strategic logistics, including energy supplies. This is no longer the case.

The cyberattacks Iran conducted on U.S. water supply sites in at least seven states were not carried out in isolation. In keeping with its longstanding military doctrine, Iranian representatives have recently threatened to target American domestic energy supplies and other strategic infrastructure.

China and Russia also include attacks on American and allied energy infrastructure in their war doctrines, and it’s past time to prepare accordingly. America must take the following four steps to protect its energy from Iran and other adversary threats.

IRANIAN HACKERS ATTACKED OUR WATER SYSTEMS. HERE ARE 5 THINGS OUR LEADERS NEED TO DO NOW

First, the U.S. should require that components for our critical infrastructure not be manufactured in China or other adversary states.

Second, the government and utilities should make secure and reliable electricity a top priority, including by influencing our choice of fuel sources.

Third, the U.S. should harden electricity systems against cyber-attacks and sabotage.

Fourth, the U.S. must develop defenses against electromagnetic attacks that disrupt and destroy electronic equipment.

TRUMP IS PROVING THAT THE WAY TO BETTER OUR MILITARY IS TO SECURE OUR SUPPLY CHAINS

The border between foreign and domestic fronts in war has completely blurred as hybrid warfare has displaced conventional conflict between militaries. Iran believes that America over-relies on technology and that attacking our energy supplies will reduce our advantages during warfare . Such attacks would affect more than our troops; power to military installations runs primarily on civilian supply lines, and disruptions to domestic electricity could trigger public panic and undermine support for necessary conflict.

It could also prevent or slow American military operations. The easiest way to stop a bomber is not to shoot it down but to make the pilot lose electricity at his home or base. Chinese military doctrine, for example, calls for attacking our domestic energy sector before invading Taiwan.

Recent years have seen multiple cases of both cyberattacks and physical sabotage of America’s domestic electricity, including the cyberattack on the Colonial Pipeline and sniper attacks on high-voltage power transformers in California, Utah, and Oregon. Unfortunately, few meaningful changes have taken place to prevent similar attacks in the future.

In fact, we have installed components in our own grids that allow China to disrupt American domestic electricity. China is the largest producer of electricity inverters, which make high-intensity current from power plants usable in homes and businesses. By remotely controlling those inverters, Beijing could trigger widespread blackouts, including to aid its Iranian ally. Chinese inverters and other Chinese components must be removed from all American electricity systems.

TRUMP'S AMBITIOUS ENERGY BET COULD BE A WINNING HAND AS THE WORLD BURNS MORE OIL, GAS THAN EVER

That’s just one way an adversary can assault our grid, however. Simply by modulating the frequency of electricity in power plants, transformers, and other infrastructure, foreign adversaries can cause fires, generate explosions, and kill personnel.

Electro-magnetic pulses (EMP) can cause even bigger and more lasting damage. China, Russia, and North Korea all have EMP capability, and Iran was reportedly close to achieving it prior to the American-Israeli offensive in June of 2025.

But not all of our grid’s security issues come from overseas. Over the last decade, the U.S. and many allies have invested heavily in renewable energy. In some places this makes sense, but in others it has added vulnerability and instability to electricity grids.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

Europe and the UK, through their net-zero policies, and Taiwan, through closing its nuclear power plants, have severely compromised their energy security and thus their physical security. If their ability to provide stable energy to their societies as well as U.S. forces operating there in wartime is compromised, so is our ability to defend them. Facing an international axis of adversaries, utilities and governments should give highest priority to security of supply of electricity.

To be clear: we have not failed — yet. In fact, our vulnerability is a product of our success. Technologically advanced militaries and societies like the U.S. and its allies have more to lose from attacks on our energy than less electrified countries like North Korea, or those with already unreliable electricity and water access like Iran. The American military is especially dependent on electricity and electronics, which are heavily integrated into communications, logistics, and weapons systems alike. These capabilities helped us become the world’s unquestioned military leader, but they must also be zealously guarded.

Attacking our energy is certainly a priority of U.S. adversaries. Protecting it must be our priority in turn.

Brenda Shaffer is a faculty member of the Energy Academic Group.

item.title: America's AI boom is a jobs opportunity, not an excuse for universal basic income
item.description: The $500 billion Stargate project and dozens more data centers are putting union electricians, pipefitters, and HVAC techs to work earning six figures.
item.content:encoded:
The same voices warning that artificial intelligence will wipe out American jobs have a ready answer: stop working and take a government check. Some call it Universal Basic Income, others call it compassion. But I believe it is a calculated insult to the dignity of work and an admission that the people who actually build, move, and power this country have no productive role left to play.

My father was a Teamster, and that fact shaped everything that came after it. My time in Congress was spent building genuine relationships with labor organizations that most Republicans had written off as unreachable. The Teamsters, Ironworkers, and numerous other unions supported my campaigns not because I told them what they wanted to hear, but because I showed up, listened, and treated their concerns as the serious policy questions they are. When President Trump named me Secretary of Labor, I remembered my father’s work and the mission handed to me felt personal.

The real fight in this country right now is not left versus right. Rather, it is whether we will respond to technological change by paying millions of workers to disappear, or whether we will put American labor to work building the largest infrastructure mobilization since the interstate highway system, including the data centers, power plants, and supply chains that will actually power the future. I know which side of that choice my father would have been on, and I know which side I am on.

A SOUTHERN STATE JUST TOOK THE TOP SPOT IN ONE OF THE WORLD’S FASTEST-GROWING INDUSTRIES

Labor unions large and small are driving an infrastructure buildout across the United States that rivals anything this country has undertaken in generations. Data centers, the physical backbone of the AI economy, are going up faster than anything we have built in recent memory. In January, the White House announced Stargate, a $500 billion private investment to build AI infrastructure across the country, and that is just one project. Dozens more are already underway. A single large facility can put 1,500 skilled tradespeople to work at peak construction, many of them clearing six figures with overtime. They accomplish this without a college degree, or student debt.

The workers building and maintaining these sites are overwhelmingly union tradespeople: electricians, pipefitters, ironworkers, HVAC technicians, and operating engineers. Electrical work alone can run 45 to 70 percent of a data center's construction budget. Nvidia's Jensen Huang has called this the "largest infrastructure buildout in human history." Micron CEO Sanjay Mehrotra, announcing a $250 billion U.S. investment commitment earlier this month, put it more plainly: "This is American investment. American technology. American workers." They're both right.

The country has a choice about how to meet this moment. The right answer is to lean in, to expand registered apprenticeships, cut the permitting red tape that slows power projects, and get serious about training the next generation of electricians and pipefitters so that real demand and real skill drive real wages. That is the winning play, and it is already underway. It rewards the trades that built the interstates and the power grid the first time around, and it rewards the regions of America that have been told for two decades that their skills were obsolete and that they should "learn to code."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

The other answer being pushed, with increasing volume, is universal basic income. The pitch is that artificial intelligence will eliminate work, so the government should write every American a check and call it compassion. It isn't compassion. It is surrender. Work is not just a paycheck. It is the thing that lets a parent stand up, look their kids in the eye, and say, "I built this."

CALIFORNIA ‘BASIC INCOME’ EXPERIMENT FAILS TO PROVIDE ‘FINANCIAL INDEPENDENCE,’ STUDY FINDS

The fight for the American worker is won by showing up year round, not just in November, and by choosing the side that builds, earns, and owns its future over the side that offers checks and excuses. The data center moment is the test, and the trades are ready, the workforce is ready, and the voters in the middle are paying very close attention.

This is a commitment to what comes next: an American economy where the people willing to build the future get to own it. The interstate builders of the 1950s didn't ask for a participation trophy, and neither will we. Let's get to work.

item.title: Russia is helping China close gap with US forces amid Taiwan tensions, warns longtime military leader
item.description: Retired Rear Adm. Mark Montgomery warns Russia is giving China submarine quieting technology that could erode a key U.S. Navy undersea advantage.
item.content:encoded:
Sound alarms are blaring over an escalating partnership between Russia and China to subvert the U.S. Military amid rising hostility between the world powers.

Rear Adm. Mark Montgomery tells Fox News Digital that Moscow may be providing Beijing with technology to make its submarines harder for the U.S. Navy to detect, potentially eroding a key military advantage in the tensions over Taiwan.

"Russia is giving incredibly important technology to China. They're allegedly giving them submarine quieting technology," Montgomery, co-author of the new book "Axis of Aggressors," told Fox News Digital.

THREE KEY REASONS WHY AMERICA CANNOT AFFORD TO LOSE TAIWAN TO COMMUNIST CHINA

Montgomery said Russian forces are providing the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) with submarine-quieting technology, an area where China has long sought to improve its capabilities. Such a transfer, he warned, could weaken a critical U.S. advantage in undersea warfare — a gap that has long favored American forces.

"Any weakening of our asymmetric advantage in undersea warfare is a big deal," he cautioned.

The Navy says its submarine force relies on technological superiority and stealth to maintain its undersea advantage, while China has continued to face weaknesses in submarine propulsion and quieting even as it rapidly modernizes its fleet.

Quieting technology reduces a submarine’s acoustic signature, making it harder to detect and track. Russian assistance in that area could help Beijing narrow the gap, complicating the U.S. Navy’s ability to find Chinese submarines in a potential future conflict over Taiwan's independence from the CCP.

The Chinese Embassy did not directly address whether Beijing has received Russian submarine-quieting technology when reached by Fox News Digital.

"Military cooperation between China and Russia consistently adheres to the principles of non-alliance, non-confrontation, and non-targeting of third parties, playing a significant role in safeguarding the sovereignty and security of both nations and maintaining international and regional peace and stability," the embassy said in a statement. "We hope that relevant parties will view China-Russia military cooperation objectively and rationally, and stop groundless speculation."

The embassy said Taiwan is China’s internal affair and urged the U.S. to safeguard stability in the bilateral relationship and across the Taiwan Strait.

Montgomery’s warning echoes concerns raised by Adm. Samuel Paparo, commander of U.S. Indo-Pacific Command, who told the Senate Armed Services Committee in April 2025 that China was receiving "potentially submarine quieting help" from Russia.

US FALLS BEHIND IN HYPERSONIC RACE AS CHINA, RUSSIA GAIN EDGE

Paparo said China’s backing of Russia’s war effort — including machine tools and legacy chips — was part of a broader exchange in which Moscow was returning assistance in military areas where it holds particular strengths.

The exchange reflects a deepening relationship in which Russia and China are increasingly providing capabilities the other lacks, Montgomery said.

"This transactional relationship is putting the United States and its most important allies and partners at risk," he said.

Paparo sounded a similar warning in November 2024, saying he expected Russia to provide China submarine technology that could help close America’s undersea advantage. He described the relationship between Moscow and Beijing as a "transactional symbiosis."

China, meanwhile, has helped Russia rebuild its defense industrial base during the war in Ukraine. Paparo told senators Beijing provided 70% of the machine tools and 90% of the legacy chips that enabled Moscow to rebuild its war machine.

Montgomery said China’s support extends beyond those supplies.

"And then China has backstopped the whole thing," Montgomery said, pointing to increased Chinese foreign direct investment and trade with Russia as well as components used in Moscow’s ballistic, cruise and hypersonic missiles.

The support has helped keep Russia’s economy and war machine operating, Montgomery argued.

In return, he said, Moscow is increasingly providing Beijing with military technology it had previously been reluctant to share — including the alleged submarine-quieting assistance.

In October 2024, the Treasury Department said a Russian defense firm coordinated production of Garpiya attack drones at factories in China, using Chinese-made engines and components before the weapons were transferred to Russia for use in Ukraine.

Russia has provided Beijing with more direct military assistance as well. A 2025 RUSI investigation, based on leaked Russian contracts and correspondence, found that Moscow agreed to equip and train a Chinese airborne battalion and transfer technology that could help Beijing develop similar capabilities itself.

Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine is now in its fifth year, with no ceasefire agreement in place despite continued diplomatic efforts. The prolonged war has deepened Moscow’s dependence on Chinese industrial and financial support while giving Russia battlefield experience and military technologies that could be valuable to Beijing in a future Taiwan contingency.

For the U.S., the stakes are particularly acute around Taiwan. American submarines are central to U.S. planning for a potential Indo-Pacific conflict, and quieter Chinese vessels could make it harder to track, deter and counter the People’s Liberation Army Navy in waters surrounding the island.

Montgomery said the possible transfer reflects the broader argument of Axis of Aggressors : America’s adversaries are increasingly trading the capabilities each lacks, creating challenges that span Europe and the Indo-Pacific.

Fox News Digital has reached out to the Russian embassy for comment. U.S. Pacific Command declined to comment.

item.title: Governments can take your stocks without your permission. It happens all the time
item.description: States are quietly rewriting unclaimed property laws, shortening dormancy periods and using inactivity standards to seize stock from investors.
item.content:encoded:
Here is some investment advice you probably haven’t heard before: If you own stock, occasionally log in and jiggle the handle. Otherwise, depending on where you live, a state may eventually decide that you have abandoned your investment.

Not because you died. Not because anyone proved you moved away. Not necessarily because your mail was returned. You may still be receiving statements. Your dividends may still be landing automatically in your bank account. You simply haven’t done anything lately.

That distinction sounds absurd. It is becoming increasingly important.

THE RICH HAVE ONE FINANCIAL HABIT MOST AMERICANS IGNORE AT THEIR PERIL

Over the last few years, states have quietly been rewriting unclaimed-property laws in ways that make securities easier to declare abandoned. The clock has gotten shorter and the definition of "abandoned" has gotten broader.

Computershare, one of the country's largest stock transfer agents, says there was a time when most states waited seven years before treating stock as abandoned. Today, more than half use three years. Even more consequential, states have increasingly shifted from a "lost" standard, such as returned mail, to an "inactivity" standard. Computershare itself calls the trend "unfortunate."

Think about what changed.

Under the old logic, the government was essentially saying: We can't find you. Under the new logic, it can be: You haven't contacted us lately. That is a radically lower bar for taking custody of somebody's investment.

WE ALL ARE DESPERATE FOR A FINANCIAL CHECK-UP. TIME TO SAY, ‘SHOW ME THE MONEY!’

And for the investor who follows the most basic rule of long-term investing, buy good companies and leave them alone, it creates a bizarre trap. Computershare warns investors that merely receiving statements or having dividends automatically deposited may not qualify as sufficient activity under some state laws.

In other words, the financial system may know exactly where your dividends go but still decide that you have disappeared. Then the machinery starts.

Your brokerage firm or transfer agent identifies the account as approaching dormancy. Notices go out. If the right kind of response doesn't arrive, the securities can be transferred to the state as unclaimed property.

And then something far more consequential can happen. The state can sell your stock.

Ask Jan Peters. Peters is a German citizen who worked for Amazon and owned 1,029 Amazon shares before the company's 20-for-1 stock split. California ended up with his shares even though Peters lived in Munich, Germany. His Supreme Court petition says his address had somehow become, "Munich, CA 00000."

California sold the Amazon stock for about $1.6 million. By June 2025, Peters calculated that those same shares would have been worth more than $4.2 million. He eventually received the sale proceeds. He did not receive the Amazon investment he had owned or its subsequent appreciation. His challenge ultimately reached the Supreme Court, which declined to hear it in October 2025.

From the state's perspective, Peters' abandoned property had been processed. From his perspective, roughly $2.6 million of investment appreciation was gone.

That raises an obvious question. Why are states making it easier for investments to enter this system? The official answer is consumer protection.

States argue, with some justification, that unclaimed-property programs act as a giant lost-and-found. Instead of leaving forgotten assets with banks and corporations indefinitely, the state takes custody and creates one central place where owners can search for them.

There is another side to the ledger, however. States get the money. Once unclaimed property reaches the government, states generally can use much of the cash while waiting for owners to appear. The liability to the owner remains, but the money itself can help finance government. And budget writers have occasionally been remarkably candid about what shorter dormancy periods mean.

In 2011, the Texas Legislative Budget Board recommended shortening several unclaimed-property dormancy periods. It projected that doing so would produce a one-time $72 million gain to the state's General Revenue Fund. The report also made the consumer argument that shorter periods could make owners easier to locate. Both things can be true.

New Jersey was even more dramatic. When it considered reducing various dormancy periods to three years, the state's Division of Taxation projected that revenue from existing unclaimed-property categories could jump from about $90 million to $309 million in one fiscal year. It separately projected another $72 million from newly covered or clarified categories, including securities.

This does not prove that every state legislator changing an unclaimed-property law is plotting a cash grab.

It proves something more important: The financial incentive is not imaginary. Governments calculate it. And everyone else in the system has incentives of their own.

Transfer agents and brokers must comply with dozens of different state laws. They need standardized procedures that can process millions of accounts cheaply and efficiently. Contractors get paid to administer unclaimed property. Brokers can get paid to take custody and sell securities. States get assets sooner when dormancy periods shrink.

The investor is the odd person out. The investor's interest may be exactly the opposite: Leave my stock alone.

And history shows that the machinery does not always get it right.

In 2006, the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) accused Bank of New York of failing to properly search for approximately 14,159 lost securityholders because of mailroom practices and computer coding errors. About $11.5 million of their assets ultimately went to states as unclaimed property.

The SEC's remedy was revealing. Bank of New York had to compensate affected investors based on the greater of the value when their assets were escheated or their later value, recognizing that an old cash value does not necessarily make an investor whole.

Then, in 2023, the SEC found problems in the lost-shareholder procedures at DST Asset Manager Solutions. Federal regulators concluded that the firm's internal screening rules prevented some potentially better addresses from being used to contact investors, putting their property at increased risk of being sent to states.

So, this isn't merely a hypothetical concern about what an automated system might do. Regulators have documented cases where the systems failed.

Meanwhile, the volume is enormous. Computershare reported 51,320 lost-securityholder accounts remitted to states in 2024 alone. That does not mean those 51,320 transfers were improper. It means this isn't some obscure process affecting a few forgotten stock certificates in somebody's attic.

It is an industrial-scale pipeline. And Washington is finally starting to ask questions.

In April, Massachusetts Democrat Sen. Elizabeth Warren asked the organization representing state unclaimed-property administrators to explain why states have been switching from returned-mail standards to inactivity standards and shortening dormancy periods.

Florida, meanwhile, has begun moving in the opposite direction. Its 2026 reforms restore returned mail or failed electronic communication as an important trigger for securities and extend an owner-inactivity period from three years to 10 years in specified circumstances.

That is closer to common sense. If I stop visiting my house for three years, I still own my house. If I leave a painting in a closet for 10 years, I still own the painting. And if I buy 500 shares of Apple and don't touch them for years, that is not evidence that I abandoned them. It may simply mean I am a patient investor.

Unclaimed-property law was created to protect owners whose property had genuinely become lost. Somewhere along the way, "lost" started becoming "inactive." And once government can treat doing nothing as evidence that you've abandoned something, the concept of ownership starts getting awfully thin.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

The rule should be simple: If you know who I am, you know where I am, and there is evidence that the account still belongs to me, my stock isn't abandoned.

It's mine. Leave it alone.

item.title: FBI touts 6,000 arrests, 44% homicide drop one year into Trump's DC crime crackdown
item.description: FBI Director Kash Patel says the Washington, D.C., crime crackdown yielded over 6,000 arrests and 1,300 illegal firearm seizures in one year.
item.content:encoded:
EXCLUSIVE: The FBI on Tuesday marked the first anniversary of the Trump administration's crime crackdown in Washington, D.C., touting thousands of arrests and seizures since the enhanced federal enforcement effort began.

The milestone comes one year after President Donald Trump launched the Safe and Beautiful initiative in Washington, increasing the federal law enforcement presence and deploying hundreds of federal agents and National Guard troops to combat crime in the nation's capital.

"Last summer President Trump made the historic decision to surge federal resources to Washington D.C. to crack down on crime – and thanks to his brilliant leadership, the work of brave FBI agents and our law enforcement partners, and the support of our Justice Department, our nation’s capital is now safer than it’s been in decades," FBI Director Kash Patel told Fox News Digital.

TRUMP’S DC LAW-AND-ORDER BLITZ MARKS ONE YEAR WITH EYE-POPPING HAUL OF SUSPECTS

"One year later, the FBI has worked with partners to make over 6,000 arrests, nearly 2,000 drug seizures, and over 1,300 illegal firearm seizures," Patel continued. "Homicides in D.C. are down an incredible 44% from last year."

The FBI said the enforcement effort has resulted in 6,121 arrests, 237 search warrants and the recovery of $252,592 in cash.

Patel vowed that the federal enforcement effort would continue.

"The greatest country on earth should have a capital city reflecting it – where American taxpayers can live, visit, and petition their government without fear of violent crime," Patel said.

TRUMP’S DC BEAUTIFICATION PUSH WINS RARE DEM PRAISE AS PRESIDENT SNAPS LANDMARKS BACK TO LIFE

"Thanks to President Trump and brave law enforcement, one year later we have made historic progress to that end, and the work will only continue," he added.

The federal surge followed a series of high-profile violent crimes in Washington, including the June 2025 killing of 21-year-old congressional intern Eric Tarpinian, the beating of a former DOGE staffer and the fatal shooting of a 14-year-old boy in a case involving alleged MS-13 gang members.

The National Guard deployment also drew criticism from Democratic leaders, including then-Washington, D.C., Mayor Muriel Bowser.

"I don't think it's legal, let me start there, for the National Guard to police Americans on American soil," Bowser said at the time.

Fox News Digital's Ashley J. DiMella contributed to this report.

item.title: Primary takeaways: Dems’ left-center battle intensifies as Schumer takes another hit; split decision for Trump
item.description: Democratic Senate Leader Sen. Chuck Schumer suffers a second straight primary setback as Peggy Flanagan wins Minnesota's Senate nomination by 20 points.
item.content:encoded:
MADISON, Wis. – For a second straight week, the progressive left-wing won a high-stakes Senate primary battle over the establishment in what is seen as a setback for longtime Democratic Senate Leader Sen. Chuck Schumer.

But the biggest ballot-box face-off between the far left and the center in the ongoing fight for the ideological future of the Democratic Party ended with a narrow victory for the establishment, as Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley defeated democratic socialist state Rep. Francesca Hong in Wisconsin's gubernatorial primary.

Meanwhile, the Democrats' generational showdown claimed another longtime member of Congress.

And it was a split decision for President Donald Trump's endorsements in statewide Republican nomination contests, as Minnesota, Wisconsin, Connecticut, Vermont, South Carolina and Alabama held primaries on Tuesday.

DEMOCRATIC GROUP LAUNCHES $15 MILLION WAR ON DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS: 'MORTAL DANGER'

Upper Midwest showdowns

"I know we don’t have the final results right now but I do know we are ready to keep fighting," Democratic gubernatorial candidate state Rep. Francesca Hong told supporters at a primary night event in Wisconsin's capital city before the race was called.

Hong, a former chef and single parent who is a Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) member, narrowly lost to Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley, who consolidated support from more mainstream Democrats and was backed by retiring Democratic Gov. Tony Evers.

Crowley will face Rep. Tom Tiffany, who cruised to the GOP nomination. Tiffany is a hard-right member of the conservative House Freedom Caucus who was backed by Trump in the primary. The general election winner will succeed Democratic Gov. Tony Evers, who decided against seeking a third term in office.

DEMOCRACY ’26: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB

Hong was backed by top nationally known progressives, including Reps. Ilhan Omar of Minnesota and Ro Khanna of California, a potential 2028 Democratic presidential contender. But two champions of the left, Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York, didn't endorse in the race.

Hong ran on a platform that includes guaranteed paid leave, boosting the state's minimum wage from $7.25 to $20 per hour, and a one-year moratorium in Wisconsin on building AI data centers. Hong has faced scrutiny over years-old social media posts calling for defunding and abolishing the police. But she says she no longer supports cutting police budgets or abolishing police departments.

She also made national headlines over the past two weeks for a resurfaced social media post from 2020 where she argued that the country should "cancel Thanksgiving" in order to "stop celebrating colonialism."

Hong walked back her Thanksgiving comments, amid backlash, and now says that Thanksgiving is her "favorite holiday."

The Democratic primary was rocked this summer, as Wisconsin Lt. Gov. Sara Rodriguez and former Lt. Gov. Mandela Barnes, two of the major contenders for the gubernatorial nomination, exited the race. And Crowley, who earlier suspended his campaign and backed Rodriguez, re-entered the contest.

MEET THE FAR LEFT INSURGENTS WAGING WAR ON THE DEMOCRATIC PARTY IN THE 2026 MIDTERMS

Crowley was backed by Evers, who joined him on the campaign trail in the closing stretch leading up to the primary, as they both questioned Hong's electability and warned that a victory by her would help Tiffany in the general election. Meanwhile, pro-GOP super PACs, including one aligned with the Republican Governors Association, shelled out millions of dollars to boost Hong in the primary, because they view her as the weakest Democratic candidate.

The final pre-primary polls indicated Hong with a healthy double-digit lead. But the polls were off again, as they were a week ago when left-wing Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed narrowly edged more moderate Rep. Haley Stevens for the party's Senate nomination in Michigan, which along with Wisconsin is a key Midwestern battleground.

While his margin was razor-thin, El-Sayed's win boosted the left. Fast-forward to this week, and progressives scored another victory, as Minnesota Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan downed moderate Rep. Angie Craig by roughly 20 points to capture the Democratic Senate nomination.

Flanagan, who was backed by top progressives including Sanders and Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts, will now face off with GOP nominee Michele Tafoya, a former longtime NBC Sports reporter, in the race to succeed retiring Democratic Sen. Tina Smith.

SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

It's been 24 years since a Republican won a U.S. Senate election in Minnesota. But Flanagan's victory may boost the GOP hopes of flipping the seat in a left-leaning but competitive state.

Craig was supported by Democratic establishment leaders including Schumer. Craig's defeat is the second major setback for Schumer in a week, following El-Sayed's victory in Michigan. And Flanagan has said that if elected in November, she wouldn't support Schumer remaining as Democratic leader in the Senate.

Democrats' generational battle

Rep. John Larson of Connecticut became the seventh House Democrat ousted so far this primary season.

Larson, who's been in Congress for nearly three decades, was defeated by double digits in the Democratic primary in Connecticut's solidly-blue 1st Congressional District by former Hartford Mayor Luke Bronin.

With both candidates touting their progressive credentials, this race was less about ideology and more about generational change in the party, which was fueled two years ago by then-81-year-old President Joe Biden's exit from the presidential race amid questions over his physical and mental stamina following a disastrous debate performance against Trump.

The 47-year-old Bronin is three decades younger than the 78-year-old Larson, who became the latest political victim of a push by Democratic voters to sweep out older incumbents and replace them with younger leaders.

"John Larson is a good man, but he's been in Congress since the 90s. The stakes are just too high to keep doing the same thing," Bronin, a retired Naval intelligence officer, argued in one of his campaign ads.

Larson countered by touting his experience and his record as a fighter in Congress.

"We are a country in absolute crisis. We need our toughest fighters. I've taken on Trump, DOGE, and ICE, and won," Larson wrote in a social media post.

Larson joined Reps. Al Green of Texas, Diana DeGette of Colorado, Adriano Espaillat of New York and Shri Thanedar of Michigan, who also fell to younger primary challengers.

The generational battle will likely play out on a larger stage in a couple of weeks, as 47-year-old Rep. Seth Moulton challenges 80-year-old Sen. Ed Markey, a progressive leader, in the party's Senate primary in Democrat-dominated Massachusetts.

Split decision for Trump

Backed by Trump, appointed Sen. Darline Graham captured the most votes in Tuesday's special Republican Senate primary in South Carolina, in the race to succeed her brother, the late Sen. Lindsey Graham.

But with no candidate topping 50% of the vote, Graham will face off in a runoff in two weeks with Rep. Ralph Norman, who came in second. Rep. Russell Fry and former Gov. and former Rep. Mark Sanford, as well as other contenders, fell short in the special primary, which was held one month to the day after the longtime senator suddenly died at age 71.

"I want to thank President Trump, his steadfast support and his complete and total endorsement means so much to me. He knows that I will stand with him and fight for his agenda, just like Lindsey did," Graham said at her primary night event.

Norman, who unsuccessfully campaigned this year for the GOP gubernatorial nomination in the race to succeed term-limited South Carolina Gov. Henry McMaster, is a Trump ally in the House and also showcased his support for the president in his Senate campaign.

Trump's sway over the GOP remains immense, and the power of his endorsements in Republican primaries faced another test in South Carolina, which the president passed.

But the Trump endorsement hasn't proven to be a sure bet this cycle in solidly-red South Carolina.

Trump backed Lt. Gov. Pamela Evette for the GOP gubernatorial nomination — in the race to succeed the term-limited McMaster — ahead of the state's early June primary.

Evette was the top vote-getter in the primary but lost the ensuing runoff election against South Carolina Attorney General Alan Wilson in a landslide. And Trump, ever hungry for a victory, endorsed Wilson in addition to Evette days before the runoff.

The big question going forward is whether Graham will suffer the same fate as Evette.

The winner of the Senate runoff election in two weeks will be considered the clear front-runner in the solidly red state in the midterms against Democratic nominee Annie Andrews, a pediatrician.

Meanwhile, Trump suffered a rare endorsement setback in Minnesota.

Mike Lindell, the MyPillow founder and former CEO who is a close Trump ally who joined the president in denying former President Joe Biden's victory in the 2020 White House race, had Trump's backing. But Lindell lost the Minnesota Republican gubernatorial primary to state House Speaker Lisa Demuth.

item.title: Heroic Florida K-9 returns to sheriff's office days after being shot protecting 3 deputies, losing leg
item.description: K-9 Ace, the Polk County German shepherd who lost a leg shielding three deputies, made an emotional return to the sheriff's office after recovering ahead of retirement.
item.content:encoded:
Less than a week after being shot and losing a leg while protecting three deputies, heroic Florida K-9 Ace was back on his feet Tuesday for an emotional return to the sheriff's office.

Ace, a 7-year-old German shepherd who has served with the Polk County Sheriff's Office since March 2020, was wounded as deputies attempted to arrest 27-year-old Angel Bowers.

Authorities said Bowers allegedly fired at least four rounds at three deputies who were attempting to arrest him after he failed to appear in court. Bowers was killed by deputies at the scene.

DEPUTY US MARSHAL FATALLY SHOT WHILE SERVING ARREST WARRANT IN LOUISIANA

Polk County Sheriff Grady Judd said Ace protected the three deputies from Bowers but was shot in his left front leg, shattering the bone and tearing an artery that caused massive blood loss.

Ace's partner and handler, Deputy Natalie Oestreich, treated his wounds and carried him to safety, according to the sheriff's office.

Ace was rushed to Parkway Veterinary Emergency Clinic in Lakeland, where he was stabilized before a Tampa General Hospital Aeromed helicopter transported him to the Veterinary Medical Center at Lakewood Ranch. Veterinarians there performed a several-hour surgery to amputate his left front leg.

On Sunday, the sheriff's office posted video showing deputies arriving at the veterinary medical center to greet an energetic Ace as he prepared to return home.

AMERICA'S WOUNDED COPS FIND HOPE, HEALING AND SECOND CHANCE THROUGH OFFICERS WHO REFUSE TO LEAVE THEM BEHIND

"Upon waking from the anesthesia, Ace attempted to walk out of there," the sheriff's office wrote. "He has not been deterred since. In fact he outran the camera attempting to film his release this afternoon!"

Video shows Ace interacting with deputies before walking out of the medical center under his own power to thunderous applause while wearing a shirt that read "ride or die."

Two days later, Ace made his first trip back to the sheriff's office since being shot in the line of duty.

"Look at Ace. He's happy; he's eating; he bit my finger," Judd said. "We are so proud of Natalie and Ace. They stood in the gap between good and evil and they saved three deputies' lives. That's why we're so proud of him. He did so good."

MAN WANTED IN DEPUTY AMBUSH CAUGHT AFTER WILDLIFE CAMERA SIGHTING AND MAJOR MANHUNT

Judd said Oestreich will spend time with Ace as he continues to recover before she returns to work. Ace, however, will retire from law enforcement.

"Chill out and enjoy your retirement Ace," Judd said.

The sheriff's office also honored Ace in a social media post, writing, "His days of chasing bad guys may be over, but Ace will always be one of our heroes!"

Polk Sheriff's Charities Inc. has established a K-9 fund to help support Ace's care. The sheriff's office said those interested in helping can donate directly to the fund through the organization's website.

item.content:encoded:
Five 17-year-old friends were killed when their vehicle plunged off a cliff and down a steep Colorado hillside, leaving their families and community grappling with an unimaginable loss just as a new school year begins.

The five boys, all from Grand Junction, were traveling along Lookout Lane late Saturday when their vehicle veered off the roadway and went down the steep incline, according to authorities.

Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., fended off four challengers in her Democratic primary on Tuesday as she heads to the general election where she will fight to retain her seat for a fifth term representing Minnesota's 5th Congressional District in the U.S. House of Representatives.

The incumbent Somali-born congresswoman faced lower profile challengers — Julie Trang Le, a former federal immigration prosecutor; Abena McKenzie, a nurse who ran against Omar in the 2024 primary, receiving just 0.38% of the vote; Latonya Reeves, DNC member and a longtime activist running from Omar's right; and Nate Schluter, a political outsider with barely any footprint in the race.

The 5th District includes Minneapolis and several nearby suburbs and is one of the most Democratic congressional districts in Minnesota.

Omar has represented the district since 2019. She was one of the first two Muslim women elected to Congress and the first Somali American elected to the House.

The one-time refugee and a founding member of the so-called Squad has become one of the Democratic Party's most prominent progressive voices. She has repeatedly drawn national attention for her positions on immigration, healthcare and U.S. policy toward Israel.

2026 MIDTERMS: PRIMARIES, KEY RACES AND ELECTION RESULTS

item.title: Schumer dealt another blow as progressive insurgency scores win in key Senate battle

Progressives again scored a victory in Minnesota where Gov. Tim Walz’s second-in-command toppled an establishment-backed member of Congress.

Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan eked out a victory over Rep. Angie Craig, D-Minn., on Tuesday, marking yet another battle won in the progressive proxy war to reshape the Democratic Party during this midterm election cycle.

Flanagan, like other progressives in the hunt for a position of power in Congress, has honed her left-leaning bona fides by backing Medicare for all and pushing an end to military aid to Israel.

REPUBLICANS GET THE DEMOCRAT THEY WANTED AS SOCIALIST ABDUL EL-SAYED WINS MICHIGAN SENATE PRIMARY

She’s also vowed to go after Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) in the wake of two deadly immigration enforcement-related shootings in Minnesota and used Craig’s support of legislation, like the Laken Riley Act, as a political cudgel to build a distinction between the two of them.

Those positions have earned her the backing of progressive heavyweights like Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., and even Sen. Tina Smith, D-Minn., whose decision to retire from the Senate opened up the contest. 

Notably, Sen. Amy Klobuchar, D-Minn., who is running for governor, has not weighed in on the race so far. 

Craig, who was viewed as the safer, more moderate pick, had the backing of the Democratic old-guard, including Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y.

BIG MONEY PROPELS DEM MEGACHURCH PASTOR TO VICTORY IN LONGSHOT KANSAS SENATE BID

Republicans are licking their chops, too, at Schumer getting handed another loss. 

"Morale among Chuck Schumer’s establishment is at an all-time low, and Bernie Sanders’ socialist flank is filling the gap with candidates like Peggy Flanagan and Abdul El-Sayed," Bernadette Breslin, a spokesperson for the National Republican Senatorial Committee, told Fox News Digital.

And it’s also brought reams of cash into the race. Craig has raised nearly $13 million this cycle, according to filings from the Federal Election Commission, while Flanagan has raked in just shy of $7 million.

"Peggy Flanagan is about bringing about real change, standing up to the big money interests," Sanders told "Face the Nation" on Sunday. "There is a reason why the super PACs and the billionaires are flooding Minnesota with all kinds of money. Same thing as Michigan."

Republicans see Flanagan’s candidacy in the same vein as Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, who last week similarly squeaked out a narrow win over Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich., who, like Craig, has Schumer’s backing.

BOMB-THROWER DEM MAKES SHOCKING PROMISE TO KICK SCHUMER TO CURB DURING SENATE DEBATE

They also have built-in messaging against her: Flanagan was Walz’s right hand as the Minnesota fraud scandal rippled across the airwaves and nation. While the scandal killed his prospects of running for reelection as governor, it has so far not kneecapped Flanagan's candidacy. And Walz hasn't waded into the endorsement game in the Senate contest, either. 

They’re confident that national Republicans’ candidate of choice, former NFL sideline reporter Michele Tafoya, will win her primary and be the candidate to turn Minnesota red. There's also the possibility that Flanagan, who has not raked in the same level of cash that Craig did, may become a resource drain for other key races on Democrats' score card. 

"Minnesota and Michigan being in play was not on Chuck Schumer’s bingo card this cycle," a GOP operative told Fox News Digital. "It remains to be seen which battleground(s) Democrats will have to pull resources from to drag socialists like Peggy Flanagan and Abdul El-Sayed across the finish line in November."

And Sen. Tim Scott, R-S.C., when asked by CNN which races kept him up at night, said one contest gave him hope.

"The one thing that gets me excited when I think about this election cycle on the map is Minnesota," said Scott, the chair of the National Republican Senatorial Committee (NRSC). "I think Minnesota, we have a real shot with Michele Tafoya."

"What we know without question is, she is within a point of the lieutenant governor right now," he said. "So if we can continue to let her show the contrast between the two candidates, I think Michele Tafoya's the kind of Republican that can win."

item.title: Minnesota House speaker Lisa Demuth wins GOP gubernatorial primary to replace Tim Walz in November
item.description: Minnesota House Speaker Lisa Demuth beat Trump-backed MyPillow CEO Mike Lindell for the GOP governor nomination to replace outgoing Gov. Tim Walz.
item.content:encoded:
Minnesota House Speaker Lisa Demuth has won the Republican gubernatorial primary and will move on to face the Democratic nominee in November to replace outgoing Gov. Tim Walz.

The victory amounts to a significant show of strength for Demuth, who stayed in the race after losing the Republican Party endorsement to Kendall Qualls at the state convention. Qualls secured the endorsement after 10 ballots, but Demuth argued that her legislative experience and record of leading House Republicans made her the party’s strongest candidate for November.

Additionally, Demuth defeated MyPillow founder and CEO Mike Lindell, who had President Donald Trump’s endorsement and has national name recognition.

No Republican has won a statewide election in the state since 2006, when Gov. Tim Pawlenty narrowly won reelection by less than a percentage point. Since then, Republicans have lost 28 consecutive statewide contests through the 2024 election, an 18-year drought that became the longest for either major party in Minnesota history.

KLOBUCHAR VOWS FRAUD CRACKDOWN, AUDIT OF MN GOV’T AS GOP BLASTS WALZ TIES

"There is hope for Minnesota, for the change that is so desperately needed," Demuth told Fox News Digital about her victory at her election night watch party in St. Paul on Tuesday night. 

"People are frustrated with fraud, they can't believe that it happened, that it was allowed to go on for so long, and so I think the message is hope, and change that is desperately needed, reducing taxes and improving education, and ending that fraud are those main messages."

The race was dramatically reshaped in January when Walz abandoned his campaign for a third term, saying he wanted to spend his final year in office focused on combating fraud in state programs rather than defending his political future.

Walz had launched his reelection campaign only months earlier, but mounting scrutiny of fraud involving government-funded programs had become a major political liability and a central line of attack from Republicans.

WALZ APPROVAL RATING CRATERS TO LOWEST LEVEL EVER AND TRAILS TRUMP AMID MASSIVE FRAUD SCANDAL: 'TIRED OF IT'

Walz’s withdrawal marked an abrupt turn for a politician who had vaulted onto the national stage less than two years earlier as Kamala Harris’ 2024 vice presidential running mate.

As governor, Walz had signed a sweeping set of Democratic priorities after his party took full control of state government, including expanded abortion protections, free school meals, legalized recreational marijuana and paid family and medical leave. But his administration also faced sustained criticism over its handling of fraud in state programs that prosecutors say could total over $9 billion.

Walz’s departure opened the governor’s race and quickly turned attention to Klobuchar as a potential successor.

Klobuchar ultimately entered the contest, transforming what had been shaping up as a referendum on Walz’s eight years in office into a race in which Republicans would instead have to take on one of Minnesota’s most established statewide politicians.

item.title: Texas Tech coach Joey McGuire says USC, Texas A&M and NC State all turned down scheduling requests
item.description: Joey Maguire says Texas Tech has been told no by USC, Texas A&M, NC State and others despite seeking top-tier non-conference schedule opponents.
item.content:encoded:
As always, the conversation around college football in the 2025-2026 offseason has revolved around strength of schedule.

Conference bragging rights are based on it. The College Football Playoff selection committee incorporates a strength of schedule and strength of resume metric into their ranking system. Perceptions of team strength can swing wildly based on assumptions of their schedule's difficulty.

Predictably, the Big Ten and SEC dominate most lists of the toughest schedules in the country in 2026. The Texas Longhorns may have the most difficult road of any team in the country. Ohio State has road trips to Texas, USC, Iowa, Nebraska and Indiana, while hosting Oregon and Michigan. It's hard to argue that's not one of the toughest schedules, even for arguably the best roster in the sport.

ESPN PERSONALITY BUSTED ON SOCIAL MEDIA FOR INACCURATELY TRYING TO PROMOTE THE SEC'S STRENGTH OF SCHEDULE

The top-to-bottom strength of the nation's two preeminent conferences, particularly the SEC, means most programs in those leagues have a reasonably demanding slate. Then there's the other Power 4 conferences.

Few would argue that the ACC or Big 12 plays the same level of schedule as Texas or Ohio State in 2026, for example. And schools in the SEC and Big Ten are happy to remind you of it. When playoff debate time comes around, they're the first to point out that 9-3 in the SEC is different from 9-3 in the Big 12. And they're usually right, at least to an extent.

But if you ask the Texas Tech Red Raiders, there's an explanation for their weaker strength of schedule, and it's because those same schools won't play them.

CODY CAMPBELL THREATENS LAWSUITS AGAINST CFB PLAYOFF, WARNS OTHER CONFERENCES AGAINST AVOIDING TEXAS TECH

Tech head coach Joey McGuire told Brett McMurphy and On3 that despite their best efforts, and conversations with big programs like USC, Texas A&M, NC State and others, they haven't been able to find top-tier opponents for their non-conference schedules moving forward.

"We’re talking to everybody and anybody. So far, everybody’s told us no," McGuire said.

There may be justifiable reasons for those teams to avoid the Red Raiders, including some residual frustration and anger over the handling of the Brandon Sorsby situation. Yet at the same time, it raises legitimate criticism of those schools, their conferences, and how they argue about this all-important metric.

Texas Tech can't make the other Big 12 teams better. But they can try to make their schedules tougher by adding matchups against traditional powerhouses like Texas A&M, USC, or Texas. If those teams won't schedule Texas Tech, how can they criticize them for not playing enough tough games?

Again, there are legitimate concerns over how Tech handled the Sorsby scandal. And McGuire has already said he wants the team to embrace the role of the "villain" in college football. Still, Tech has made major investments in improving their program, building a playoff contender, and competing with the best of the best. Instead of running away, teams should give them a chance to prove that they're reaching that next level.

Or don't complain about it later.

Democrats in deep blue Vermont have a new nominee as they take a sixth straight shot at trying to oust popular Republican Gov. Phil Scott.

item.title: Dems eye pick-up in Wisconsin swing district as Rep Van Orden set for rematch in key House race
item.description: Rebecca Cooke won Wisconsin's 3rd Congressional District Democratic primary, setting up a rematch with Republican Rep. Derrick Van Orden this fall.
item.content:encoded:
A former waitress, small-business owner and nonprofit founder won the Democratic primary in Wisconsin's 3rd Congressional District on Tuesday, setting her up for a rematch with Republican Rep. Derrick Van Orden.

Rebecca Cooke, raised on an Eau Claire-area dairy farm, defeated former Eau Claire City Council President Emily Berge on Tuesday evening. The win puts Cooke back on the ballot in one of Democrats’ top House pickup opportunities this fall.

It will be Cooke’s third attempt to win the western Wisconsin seat. She lost the 2022 Democratic primary to then-state Sen. Brad Pfaff before securing the party’s nomination in 2024. Van Orden defeated her that November by roughly 11,000 votes, winning 51.4% of the vote to Cooke’s 48.6%.

WISCONSIN DEM TOUTS ENDORSEMENT FROM UNION PUSHING BACK AGAINST CDL CRACKDOWNS ON ILLEGAL ALIEN TRUCKERS

Cooke has sought to make her working-class background central to her campaign. She grew up on a dairy farm near Eau Claire, has worked as a waitress since she was a teenager and founded the Red Letter Grant, a nonprofit supporting women entrepreneurs. She also previously operated a small retail business and served on the board of the Wisconsin Economic Development Corp. after being appointed by Democratic Gov. Tony Evers.

Her campaign has focused on affordability, health care and the economic challenges facing rural communities, while portraying Cooke as a pragmatic Democrat able to appeal across party lines in a district that includes Eau Claire, La Crosse and much of western Wisconsin.

Cooke entered the primary as the better-funded candidate and with national support from Democrats.

The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee (DCCC) added Cooke to its "Red to Blue" program, which directs party resources toward candidates viewed as viable in competitive districts.

Berge, a mental health counselor and former Eau Claire City Council president, ran as a local alternative to Cooke, arguing voters should have a choice rather than see the nomination effectively decided by national party backing and fundraising. Her strongest base of support was expected to be in and around Eau Claire.

IOWA DEM ADMITS BEING ‘UNCOMFORTABLE’ WITH WHITENESS AS SHE SEEKS TO FLIP COMPETITIVE HOUSE SEAT

The general election is likely to renew scrutiny of Cooke’s personal finances and past political work. Van Orden’s campaign has pressed her to release a financial disclosure that was extended until Aug. 13, two days after the primary. The campaign has argued that earlier disclosures showing income from political consulting and rental properties undercut Cooke’s working-class image.

Republicans have also sought to cast Cooke as a Democratic political insider, pointing to her work on Democratic campaigns and fundraising. Cooke has presented that experience as part of a broader record that includes operating a business, leading a nonprofit and working in the hospitality industry.

Van Orden, a retired Navy SEAL who was first elected in 2022, is seeking a third term.

The 3rd district in Wisconsin, a swing state, has leaned Republican in recent presidential elections, but Cooke’s narrow 2024 loss and substantial fundraising have made the race a closely watched contest as Democrats seek to win back the House in November.

The bipartisan Cook Political Report moved the race from "lean Republican" in the last election cycle to "toss up."

item.title: Chiefs receiver Rashee Rice says he is '100% locked in' after serving 30-day jail time for probation violation
item.description: Rashee Rice called his 30-day jail sentence for a THC probation violation a "reality check" as he looks ahead with Patrick Mahomes and the Chiefs at training camp.
item.content:encoded:
Before Rashee Rice was back with his Kansas City Chiefs teammates for the upcoming season, he had to serve 30 days in jail following a probation violation stemming from a multi-vehicle crash back in 2024.

Rice called the discipline a "reality check."

"It was a learning experience and a reality check," Rice said, via ESPN. "Don’t focus on the past. Focus on what’s going on now. I’m doing [well] mentally."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

Rice was on probation for his involvement in the 2024 multi-vehicle crash, where he eventually pleaded guilty to two felony charges.

The NFL also docked Rice six games for violating their personal conduct policy, which he served this past season.

CHIEFS RECEIVER RASHEE RICE JAILED FOR 30 DAYS AFTER PROBATION VIOLATION AND IT COULD GET WORSE

Rice violated his probation after testing positive for THC, which mandated a 30-day jail sentence in Texas. He began serving that sentence on May 19, and he was released from jail in mid-June.

He also received surgery to take care of loose bodies in his right knee, which caused him inflammation during his eight games for the Chiefs in 2025.

He declined to speak with reporters who were waiting for him outside the detention center, but now at training camp, Rice faced the music.

"It was mentally tough. They gave me ways to communicate with my teammates still as well as my athletic trainer," Rice explained. "Besides the hard times in there, I kept my mind right watching shows and as much Kevin Hart as I could to laugh."

Rice added that he was allowed to get treatment done on his knee while serving his time as well.

"I would stretch it, do some activation on it and then hit the weight room and jog, just condition and get the muscle fatigue going as well as my stamina."

Rice is only entering Year 4 in the NFL, but off-the-field issues have taken away from the solid chemistry he has with quarterback Patrick Mahomes, who has trusted him with top wide receiver duties. His production has warranted that as well.

"I’m 100% locked in on what’s going on now with the team," Rice explained. "I’m ready to go out there and dominate. I’ve got a good group of brothers behind me."

Rice tallied 571 yards on 53 receptions with five touchdowns in his eight games with the Chiefs in 2025. He had a breakout rookie campaign with 938 yards on 79 catches with seven scores in 2023, but he was unable to play a full year in 2024 after suffering a season-ending knee injury.

item.title: Longtime anti-Trump Dem ousted after tough primary from upstart progressive mayor

item.content:encoded:
Fourteen-term Rep. John Larson, D-Conn., met his match in Hartford Mayor Luke Bronin during Tuesday’s hard-fought primary race.

Larson, who has served in Congress since the Clinton administration, faced three challengers: Bronin, state Rep. Jillian Gilchrest and Hartford Education Board member Ruth Fortune. The sprawling district includes Hartford, Glastonbury, Bristol and Windsor Locks.

Earlier this term, during a markup of legislation providing House members with DOGE access to Treasury payment information, Larson erupted at his colleagues and began yelling:

"You will do whatever Elon Musk and Donald Trump tell you to do. Where's the independence of the committee? Where's the legislature? We're an equal branch of government," Larson yelled. "Look at the empty seats here. Where's Elon Musk?"

HOUSE DEMOCRAT LASHES OUT WHEN GRILLED ON WHETHER SOCIALIST VICTORIES WOULD THREATEN DEM UNITY

Larson has routinely criticized Musk and President Donald Trump during his tenure, notably filing more than a dozen articles of impeachment following the arrest and extraction of Venezuelan leader Nicolas Maduro.

In that case, Larson accused Trump of piracy and other offenses. The impeachment push came as Larson faced a primary challenge from the younger Bronin.

Bronin, who also served in the Obama administration, appeared to be gaining on incumbent Larson as the year went on. He ran as a candidate seeking generational change in a longtime Democratic seat.

STATE OF PLAY: DEMS BATTLE FOR SHOT AT CRUCIAL ARIZONA HOUSE SEAT AMID GOP'S RAZOR-THIN MAJORITY

The First District has not seen a Republican lawmaker since Rep. Edwin May Jr., R-Conn., who served during the Eisenhower administration.

Gilchrest is considered a progressive who also is also pro-choice abortion rights.

Fortune, considered the lowest-funded major candidate, ran an education-focused campaign.

Republican challenger Amy Chai, a medical doctor focused on addiction treatment, said on her campaign site that Americans are too stressed and depressed because of national divisions and need a change.
